Family Health

Yoga during and after breast cancer treatment

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Some people find gentle yoga helpful for fatigue, sleep and the emotional strain of breast cancer. Others prefer walking, rehabilitation exercises or a different relaxation practice. The useful question is which activity fits your treatment and recovery today, rather than whether you can complete a standard sequence.

What yoga may help with

Yoga combines movement, attention and breathing. Studies in cancer survivors, especially those treated for breast cancer, suggest that gentle programmes may improve some symptoms and quality of life. A benefit in a supervised programme does not establish that every class or individual pose produces the same result.

Evidence also differs by treatment phase and outcome. The 2024 ASCO–SIO fatigue guideline allows yoga as an option after treatment, especially for women with breast cancer, but found insufficient evidence to recommend it for or against fatigue during active treatment. That uncertainty is different from saying nobody may practise during treatment; suitability remains individual.

Keep supportive exercise separate from cancer treatment

Physical activity contributes to general health and is associated with better outcomes in some cancer populations. Its effects on weight, metabolism and hormones are among the mechanisms researchers study. That does not prove a particular yoga sequence changes insulin or oestrogen enough to prevent recurrence.

Yoga does not destroy a tumour or replace surgery, radiotherapy, endocrine treatment, chemotherapy or targeted treatment. Continue oncology follow-up and prescribed care. If cancer returns or fatigue persists, it is not evidence that you failed to exercise or think positively enough.

Ask what movement is appropriate at this stage

Useful activity may be possible before, during and after treatment, but the plan can change. Discuss recent surgery or reconstruction, healing wounds, drains, shoulder movement, radiotherapy skin changes and any chemotherapy port. Ask for practical limits on reaching, weight through the arms, lifting and getting down to the floor.

Bone metastases, fragile bones, numb feet, poor balance, severe fatigue or anaemia may require a different approach. A cancer physiotherapist or rehabilitation professional can translate those issues into specific movements. Feeling energetic on one day does not cancel a surgical restriction, and being tired is not a reason to assume all movement must stop.

Lymphoedema calls for adaptation, not automatic inactivity

Lymph-node treatment can affect fluid drainage from the arm or chest. Appropriate movement is often part of managing lymphoedema, with gradual progression and attention to symptoms. Ask your specialist how to use any prescribed compression garment during activity.

Stop and seek advice about new or increased swelling, heaviness, tightness or discomfort. A pose advertised as opening the chest is not a replacement for assessed swelling care. There is no established basis for promising that one fish pose clears breast lymph or removes scar tissue.

Prepare a comfortable place and suitable instruction

Choose comfortable clothing and a stable, non-slip surface. A secure chair, cushions or folded blankets may be more useful than trying to reproduce a photograph on the floor. Check that supports will not slip and that you can get into and out of the position without straining.

Look for a teacher with recognised training and experience adapting practice after cancer, who respects your clinical instructions. Begin with short sessions and permission to rest. A gentle or restorative label does not guarantee suitability; hot classes, fast transitions and prolonged holds can place very different demands on the body.

Cat–cow: consider the spine and the weight through your arms

Cat–cow alternates a small spinal arch with a rounded back, usually coordinated with breathing. The familiar floor version starts on hands and knees, placing weight through the wrists and shoulders while the trunk and pelvis move. That load may be unsuitable after breast surgery or with particular bone or joint problems.

If your rehabilitation professional approves it, a seated version can be easier: sit securely with the feet supported and hands resting on the thighs, then make a small comfortable movement through the trunk while breathing normally. Keep the neck relaxed and return to neutral between movements. Do not force a deep arch or chase ten repetitions. The aim is comfortable movement, not a promised change in spinal-fluid circulation.

Seated side stretch: reduce the reach when needed

A side bend involves the trunk and muscles between and around the ribs. A full overhead reach also asks the shoulder and chest tissues to lengthen. Neither kneeling on the floor nor reaching the forearm all the way to the ground is necessary to obtain a modest stretch.

Once cleared for this movement, use a stable chair or a supported seated position. Keep the pelvis steady, make a small sideward movement and stay within the shoulder range your team allows. The upper hand can remain low instead of reaching overhead. Breathe comfortably, return upright slowly and assess each side separately. Stop with sharp pain, pulling at a wound or increased symptoms rather than holding for a required number of breaths.

Supported fish pose: comfort matters more than the shape

The traditional fish shape extends the spine and neck and opens the front of the chest. Supports can lessen effort, but a high bolster or an unsupported head can still create a substantial stretch. Recent surgery, reconstruction, neck trouble or bone involvement may make the pose inappropriate.

Ask your physiotherapist to show a suitable supported resting position if you want this part of a practice. It may mean a small support, a comfortably supported head and arms kept below shoulder height, or an entirely different position. Do not drop the head backwards or insist on staying for ten minutes. Plan how to rise without loading a healing arm; use the movement method your team has taught.

Relaxation breathing can remain gentle

For a simple relaxation practice, sit comfortably or lie in a supported position that does not strain the chest. If comfortable, rest a hand lightly over the abdomen and notice the movement as you breathe in and out. Allow the breath to settle rather than forcing the lungs to fill as much as possible.

A few easy breaths may be enough. There is no need to hold your breath for as long as you can, match a rigid count or complete several sessions every day. Stop if you become dizzy, breathless or uncomfortable. Relaxation may feel helpful without a claim that it lowers your oxygen needs or sends a measured extra amount of oxygen to the brain.

Radiotherapy breath-hold is a separate clinical technique

Deep inspiration breath hold, or DIBH, may be used during breast or chest-wall radiotherapy to increase the distance between the heart and the treatment area. The team assesses its usefulness during planning; not everyone needs or can use it.

Radiographers teach the timing and monitor position and breathing during treatment. Practise only as instructed for your own plan, and tell them if it is difficult. Ordinary yoga breathing at home does not itself shield the heart or lungs from radiation, and holding longer is not automatically better protection.

Build a routine around your response

Start below the level that feels like a challenge and notice how you feel later that day and the next. You can omit a movement, practise only supported rest, or substitute the rehabilitation exercises you have been given. Exact repetition counts and long holds from a general routine are not recovery targets.

Keep progression gradual and account for treatment days, sleep and other daily activities. A brief note about pain, energy, swelling or ease of reaching may help a review appointment. Yoga does not necessarily provide all the strengthening or aerobic activity you need, so discuss the wider plan rather than treating it as a complete exercise prescription.

Know when to stop and contact the team

Stop for sharp pain, dizziness, new weakness, increasing arm swelling or symptoms that persist after practice. Tell the care team about fatigue that is severe or interferes with ordinary activities; anaemia, infection, pain, sleep problems or other causes may need assessment.

New chest pain, fainting, severe breathlessness or sudden neurological symptoms need urgent medical attention. Do not use breathing exercises to delay that assessment. After cancer treatment, a new symptom should not automatically be blamed on an unfamiliar stretch.

Make room for preference and support

An enjoyable activity is more likely to fit real life than a programme that feels like another obligation. Ask your cancer centre about affordable adapted classes or rehabilitation services. In-person guidance can be useful when learning a movement or adapting it after surgery.

You can benefit from support without choosing yoga at all. Walking, a clinician-led movement plan, counselling or another relaxation method may suit you better. Comfort, function and a workable routine matter more than completing a pose that someone else can do.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Gentle yoga can be a supportive option, but evidence varies by symptom, treatment phase and programme. The fatigue guideline’s post-treatment option should not be presented as an equally established recommendation during active treatment.

Movement choices after surgery, with lymphoedema or with bone involvement need individual adaptation. The four topics here explain options and precautions rather than prescribe an oncology rehabilitation sequence.

How BeMama can help

A short wellbeing record can help describe fatigue or movement difficulties at follow-up. It cannot decide surgical restrictions or assess swelling.

When to seek help

Stop for new pain, dizziness, weakness or swelling and contact the care team. Chest pain, severe breathlessness, fainting or sudden neurological symptoms require urgent assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Yoga may support comfort and wellbeing alongside cancer care.
  • Adapt practice to treatment, healing, bone health and symptoms.
  • A supported pose is not automatically safe for every person.
  • No pose is an established scar-removal or lymphoedema cure.
  • Radiotherapy breath-hold follows an individual monitored plan.

Frequently asked questions

Can yoga treat breast cancer itself?

No. It is supportive activity and does not replace oncology treatment or follow-up.

Is its fatigue benefit equally established during and after treatment?

No. The 2024 ASCO–SIO guideline allows yoga as a post-treatment option but found insufficient evidence for a fatigue recommendation during active treatment.

Must I wait until all treatment has ended to move?

Not necessarily. Appropriate activity is often possible during treatment, with individual restrictions and adaptations.

Can I do hands-and-knees cat–cow after surgery?

Only if that arm loading and spinal movement fit your recovery instructions. Ask about a seated alternative.

Do side stretches require an overhead arm?

No. Keep the arm and trunk within the range your care team permits; a smaller supported movement may be appropriate.

Will supported fish pose drain lymph or remove scars?

That specific promise is not established. Get a rehabilitation or lymphoedema assessment for swelling or restricted movement.

Should I avoid every activity if I have lymphoedema?

No. Suitable movement can help, but progression, symptoms and prescribed compression need an individual plan.

Do I need to hold my breath during relaxation?

No. Gentle comfortable breathing is enough; stop if it makes you dizzy or breathless.

Does home breathing practice protect me from radiotherapy exposure?

Not by itself. DIBH is assessed, taught and monitored by the radiotherapy team for the treatment plan.

What if yoga makes me feel worse?

Stop and review the symptoms with your team. Another activity may suit you better; completing yoga is not a requirement for recovery.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
